extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO examiners, and applicants dealing with patent term extension under 35 U.S.C. §156
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining eligibility, filing, and scope of patent term extensions (PTE) under 35 U.S.C. §156 and implementing regulations (37 CFR §§1.710–1.740). Covers definitions, timing, required contents, procedural roles, and statutory/regulatory exceptions and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 156(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of a patent which claims a product, a method of using a product, or a method of manufacturing a product shall be extended from the original expiration date if: (1) the patent has not expired before an application under subsection (d)(1) was filed; (2) the term of the patent has never been extended under subsection (e)(1); (3) an application for extension is submitted by the owner of record or its agent and in accordance with subsection (d) requirements; (4) the product has been subject to a regulatory review period before its commercial marketing or use; and (5) except as provided in (B) or (C), the permission for commercial marketing or use after such regulatory review period is the first permitted commercial marketing or use of the product under the provision of law under which such regulatory review period occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory checklist (35 U.S.C. 156(a)(1)-(5)) is the primary eligibility test: the applicant must demonstrate each listed element (timing, prior extensions, proper filer, regulatory review, and first permitted marketing/use). Subparts (B) and (C) provide limited exceptions (e.g., recombinant DNA manufacturing and certain animal drug approvals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "product" (35 U.S.C. 156(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'product' means: (A) the active ingredient of a new human drug, antibiotic drug, or human biological product, including any salt or ester of the active ingredient, as a single entity or in combination with another active ingredient; or (B) the active ingredient of a new animal drug or veterinary biological product that is not primarily manufactured using recombinant DNA/RNA or similar site-specific genetic manipulation techniques, including any salt or ester, as a single entity or in combination; or (C) any medical device, food additive, or color additive subject to regulation under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For PTE purposes 'product' focuses on the active ingredient (and salts/esters), not necessarily the entire formulation. Animal drugs primarily manufactured via certain biotechnology processes are excluded. See 21 CFR 60.3(b) for related definitions (active ingredient, drug product, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "drug product" and active ingredient presence
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'drug product' means the active ingredient of a given drug product (human or animal as defined) including any salt or ester, as a single entity or in combination. The active ingredient must be present in the final dosage form prior to administration to the patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility hinges on the active ingredient as approved and listed on the drug's label. Different forms (salt vs ester, enantiomer vs racemate) can constitute different drug products for extension purposes. A deesterified metabolite is generally not the same product as the approved ester form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major health or environmental effects test definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'major health or environmental effects test' means a test reasonably related to evaluation of health or environmental effects of a product which requires at least six months to conduct, and whose data is submitted to receive permission for commercial marketing or use. Periods of analysis or evaluation of test results are not included in determining the six-month period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory definition (35 U.S.C. 156(f)(3)) is used when calculating the regulatory review period; only the conduct period counts toward the six months threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing — sixty-day filing period and AIA/business-day rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for extension under 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(1) must be submitted by the owner of record or its agent within the sixty-day period beginning on the date the product received permission for commercial marketing or use under the law governing the regulatory review period. The America Invents Act clarifies that if permission is transmitted after 4:30 P.M. Eastern Time or on a non-business day, the product is deemed to receive permission on the next business day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict calendar timing governs PTE filings; applicants must compute the 60-day window using business-day rules. Special 'covered date' rules apply for controlled-substances-related approvals per the Improving Regulatory Transparency for New Medical Therapies Act (see subsection (i) and the 'covered date' definition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application contents required by 35 U.S.C. 156(d)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension application must contain: (A) the identity of the approved product and the Federal statute under which regulatory review occurred; (B) the identity of the patent and each claim which claims the approved product or a method of using/manufacturing it; (C) information enabling the Director to determine eligibility, the rights to be derived from the extension, and enabling the Director and the Secretary to determine the period of extension; (D) a brief description of activities undertaken during the regulatory review period and significant dates; and (E) such patent or other information as the Director may require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed factual support (patent claims, dates, regulatory interactions). The Office may require additional documents. Failure to include required items can render the application noncompliant under §1.740.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant identity and signature formalities (37 CFR 1.730)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application must be submitted by the owner of record or its agent and must comply with §1.740. If submitted by the patent owner, it must be signed by the patent owner or by a registered practitioner on behalf of the owner. If submitted by an agent (e.g., licensee), it must be signed by a registered practitioner on behalf of the agent. The Office may require proof of authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power of attorney for an 'Extension Application' document does not alter underlying patent powers. Registered practitioners submitting for an owner/agent must be able to show authority to act on behalf of the owner/agent if requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.710 — Patents subject to extension (CFR product definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is eligible for extension if it claims a product as defined in §1.710(b) (active ingredient of new human drug/antibiotic/human biological product including salts/esters; active ingredient of certain animal drugs not primarily manufactured via certain biotech processes; or any medical device, food additive, or color additive subject to FDA regulation) either alone or in combination or claims a method of using or manufacturing such a product, and meets other conditions of the subpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.710 restates the statutory 'product' boundaries in regulatory language used by USPTO; applicants should map claim language to §1.710(b) categories to assess eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.720 — Conditions for extension (CFR checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of a patent may be extended if: (a) the patent claims a product or method as defined in §1.710; (b) the term has never been previously extended except for extensions per §§1.701,1.760,1.790; (c) an application is submitted in compliance with §1.740; (d) the product was subject to a regulatory review period as defined in 35 U.S.C.156(g); (e) the product has received permission for commercial marketing/use and meets first-permission rules (including special rules for recombinant manufacturing and certain animal drugs); (f) application filed within the sixty-day period beginning on date of first permission (with special timing for recombinant manufacturing/animal drug situations); (g) the patent term has not expired before submission in compliance with §1.741; and (h) no other patent term has been extended for the same regulatory review period for the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This CFR checklist operationalizes the statutory requirements and adds procedural conditions (filing compliance sections and expiration checks). Applicants must satisfy each listed subcondition and follow associated filing provisions (§1.740, §1.741).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory review period — scope and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulatory review period must be a statutory regulatory review period (e.g., approvals under sections 505, 512, 515, 351) as defined in the statute; a 510(k) submission is not a regulatory review period that gives rise to eligibility for PTE. For medical devices, regulatory review for PTE must be under section 515 (Class III/HDE contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all FDA interactions count. Applicants must identify the specific Federal statute/regulatory pathway that generated the review period being relied on for PTE. Case law and PTO precedents (e.g., In re Nitinol Medical Technologies; Baxter Diagnostics) clarify that 510(k) pathways are excluded, and Congress intended only certain devices to be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: First permitted commercial marketing or use requirement (35 U.S.C.156(a)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: The approval under the relevant provision must be the first permitted commercial marketing or use of the product under the provision of law, except as provided in the statutory exceptions (e.g., recombinant DNA manufacturing and certain animal drug approvals). For human drug products the approval of the active ingredient must be the first permitted commercial marketing/use of that active ingredient as a single entity or in combination under the provision of law under which review occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This element focuses on whether the active ingredient (or specific form such as salt/ester/enantiomer) has been previously approved. Different forms can be different products (e.g., ester vs salt; enantiomer vs racemate). Combinations and ratios have nuanced treatments (a different ratio is not necessarily a different active ingredient). Prior approvals of combinations or related molecules can bar or allow extension depending on whether the active ingredient (or salt/ester) itself was previously approved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal drug special rules for subsequent approvals (35 U.S.C.156(a)(5)(C) / 37 CFR 1.720(e)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent directed to a new animal drug or veterinary biological product may be extended based on a second or subsequent approval of the active ingredient if: (A) the patent claims the drug/product; (B) the drug/product is not covered by the claims in any other patent that has been extended; (C) the patent term was not extended based on regulatory review for use in non-food-producing animals; and (D) the second/subsequent approval was the first permitted commercial marketing/use for administration to a food-producing animal. The application must be filed within sixty days of that first approval for food-producing animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows PTE for later approvals specifically for food-producing animals even if there was prior approval for non-food-producing animals, provided the listed conditions are met and filing timing is respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only one patent may be extended per regulatory review period; election required if multiple applications
rubrics_metrics.description: If more than one application for patent term extension is filed based upon a single regulatory review period, an election among the patents will be required to choose a single patent for extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and their counsel should coordinate filings because the Office will require selection of a single patent tied to the regulatory review period; see MPEP §2761 for election procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of rights during the extended period (35 U.S.C.156(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights derived from extension under 35 U.S.C.156(a) are defined in 156(b) and are not limited to a claim-by-claim basis; the statute indicates that 'the term of a patent which claims a product, a method of using a product, or a method of manufacturing a product shall be extended.' However, if the patent claims other products in addition to the approved product, the exclusive patent rights to the additional products expire with the original expiration date of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extension is attached to the patent term and the rights during the extended period are limited to the approved product (e.g., active ingredient, salts/esters). Case law (e.g., Biogen v. Banner) constrains scope (metabolites not covered), and Genetics Institute/other cases discuss claim scope implications. Applicants must identify which claims 'claim the approved product' to determine the rights conferred by the extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of extension contingent on underlying patent validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent term extension under 35 U.S.C.156 'is valid so long as the extended patent is otherwise valid without the extension.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTE does not immunize an invalid patent. Obviousness-type double patenting cannot be used to negate PTE when the potential reference patent could not have been used to challenge the unextended term of the patent that received the extension (see Novartis AG v. Ezra Ventures and Merck v. Hi-Tech Pharmacal discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer and previous-extension exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be extended under 35 U.S.C.156 even though it has been terminally disclaimed. 37 CFR 1.720(b) explains that PTE is available only if the term has never been previously extended except for extensions issued pursuant to §§1.701 (administrative delay), 1.760 (interim extension under 156(e)(2)), or 1.790 (interim extension under 156(d)(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimers that limit term under 35 U.S.C.154(b) do not automatically preclude extension under §156; PTO practice and case law (Merck, etc.) govern interactions with double-patenting and disclaimers. Applicants should evaluate prior extensions and administrative adjustments when assessing eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO and agency procedural roles and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director initially determines formal completeness and eligibility and must notify the Secretary of Agriculture or the Secretary of Health and Human Services of a complying application within sixty days and submit a copy. The Secretary then has not later than thirty days after receipt to determine the length of the applicable regulatory review period and notify the Director. If eligible, the Director calculates the length of extension and issues a Certificate of Extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the interagency timeline is important for applicants to know that the PTO relies on the appropriate executive agency (HHS/FDA or Agriculture) to determine the regulatory review period length and that statutory deadlines (60-day filing, 30-day Secretary response) affect processing.
